rows.description: A toddler's emotion flashes on quickly and off just as fast, from tantrum to giggle within minutes. Short displays move on with distraction, while lasting ones suggest a need or a health issue.

A preschooler wails theatrically over a small bump or squeals with over-large delight. Exaggeration often seeks attention or shows big feelings without control, and a calm response teaches proportion.

rows.subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
rows.subtype: Staying calm and finding an exit [Response]
rows.description: A person in a crowd notes exits, keeps their arms up and moves with the flow, not against it. Planning ahead and staying calm protects them and others around them.

rows.subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
rows.description: A friend messages the target privately, helps them stop reading comments and, if needed, reports abuse. Steady human contact matters more than public defence.

rows.subtype: Likes and dislikes as strong assertions [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler shows likes and dislikes by grabbing, refusing food or saying "mine" and "no". Firm refusal expresses growing independence and preference rather than defiance alone.

A teenager states likes and dislikes about touch, photos, sharing and closeness, and expects a "no" to be respected. Everyone has the right to refuse; adults and peers should stop and a trusted adult should be told if a refusal is ignored.

A young professional asks for deadline clarity, breaks, accommodations or leave and states preferences on how to be contacted. Framing a need with a reason and an alternative usually gets a better hearing.

A toddler bounces with delight, stamps feet in frustration or runs in circles from excitement. Whole-body motion often shows feeling before language does; naming it, for instance you are so happy, builds emotional words.

rows.subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
rows.description: A schoolchild paces before a test or bounces a leg while waiting. It can signal nerves, excitement or need for movement, and a child with a lot of energy is not necessarily defiant; movement breaks often help focus.

A teenager dances in a group, at a wedding baraat, on a practice reel or at a school event to show joy and belonging. Styles vary by culture and gender norms; pressure to perform or teasing can turn joy into shame, so choice matters.
A toddler waves, says bye-bye or babbles hello to show recognition and social interest. Shyness may lead to hiding instead, so adults do not force a greeting.

rows.subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
rows.description: A child says hello, offers a seat, shares a snack or shows the new student around. Warm welcoming teaches inclusion, and shy children can still welcome with a smile or wave.

A young adult in an interview or new college introduces self with name, role and a short line about interests. Confident, clear greetings build trust, and norms differ across cultures for title use and eye contact.

Playful teasing among friends can shift into mocking or ridicule when one person is hurt or cannot laugh along. Watching the target's face, the power balance and repetition helps children tell fun from unkind, and they should tell an adult about ongoing harm.

A young adult may face "Do this or I leave" from a friend, partner or family member. Some ultimatums state a real boundary, others are pressure or control; consider whether choices are respected and seek support if fear or coercion is present.
